note: Curated internship-level technical questions. Key points list what a good answer covers; keywords (lower-case, prefix-matched) support deterministic scoring. No external links.

Python.question: What is the difference between a list and a tuple in Python?

key_points.point: Lists are mutable; tuples are immutable
Tuples whose items are hashable can be dictionary keys; lists cannot
Lists use square brackets, tuples use parentheses

Python.explanation: Immutability makes tuples safer for fixed data; a tuple is hashable (and usable as a key) only if all its items are hashable.

Python.question: Explain list comprehensions and generators. When would you use a generator?

key_points.point: A list comprehension builds a whole list in one expression
A generator yields items lazily, one at a time
Generators save memory for large or infinite sequences

Python.explanation: Generators avoid materialising every item in memory.

Python.question: What are decorators in Python and how would you write one?

key_points.point: A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a new function
It adds behaviour without changing the original code (e.g. logging, timing, auth)
Applied with the @ syntax; functools.wraps keeps metadata

Python.explanation: Decorators are a clean way to apply cross-cutting concerns.

Java.question: What is the difference between an interface and an abstract class in Java?

key_points.point: A class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class
Abstract classes can have state (fields) and constructors
Interfaces define a contract; default methods allow some implementation

Java.explanation: Choose interfaces for capabilities, abstract classes for shared base behaviour.

Java.question: Explain how a HashMap works internally.

key_points.point: Keys are hashed with hashCode to find a bucket
Collisions are handled in the bucket (linked list or tree)
equals is used to find the exact key; average O(1) lookup

Java.explanation: Correct hashCode and equals are essential for HashMap keys.

Java.question: How does garbage collection work in Java, and what can still cause memory leaks?

key_points.point: The JVM frees objects that are no longer reachable
Generational collection: young and old generations
Leaks happen when references are kept unintentionally (static collections, listeners, caches)

Java.explanation: GC removes unreachable objects, not unused but still-referenced ones.

C++.question: What is the difference between a pointer and a reference in C++?

key_points.point: A pointer can be null and reassigned; a reference cannot
A reference is an alias for an existing object
Pointers need dereferencing with * or ->

C++.explanation: References are safer aliases; pointers are more flexible.

C++.question: What is RAII and why is it important in C++?

key_points.point: Resource acquisition is initialization: resources are tied to object lifetime
The destructor releases the resource automatically
Prevents leaks, including when exceptions are thrown; smart pointers use it

C++.explanation: RAII makes cleanup deterministic and exception-safe.

C++.question: Explain move semantics in modern C++.

key_points.point: Move transfers resources instead of copying them
Uses rvalue references (&&) and std::move
Move constructor / move assignment improve performance

C++.explanation: Moving avoids expensive deep copies of temporary objects.

JavaScript.question: What is the difference between let, const and var?

key_points.point: let and const are block-scoped; var is function-scoped
const cannot be reassigned
var is hoisted and initialised as undefined; let and const are hoisted but cannot be used before their declaration (temporal dead zone)

JavaScript.explanation: Prefer const, then let; avoid var in modern code.

JavaScript.question: Explain promises and async/await in JavaScript.

key_points.point: A promise represents a future value that resolves or rejects
async/await lets you write asynchronous code that reads sequentially
Errors are handled with .catch or try/catch

JavaScript.explanation: async/await is syntax built on top of promises.

JavaScript.question: Explain the JavaScript event loop.

key_points.point: JavaScript runs on a single thread with a call stack
Callbacks wait in task queues until the stack is empty
Microtasks (promises) run before macrotasks (timers)

JavaScript.explanation: The event loop enables non-blocking behaviour on one thread.

TypeScript.question: What does TypeScript add on top of JavaScript?

key_points.point: Static type checking at compile time
It compiles to plain JavaScript
Better tooling: autocomplete and early error detection

TypeScript.explanation: Types catch many bugs before the code runs.

TypeScript.question: What is the difference between an interface and a type alias in TypeScript?

key_points.point: Both describe object shapes
Interfaces can be extended and merged (declaration merging)
Type aliases can also name unions, primitives and tuples

TypeScript.explanation: Use interfaces for object contracts and types for unions and compositions.

TypeScript.question: Explain generics in TypeScript with an example.

key_points.point: Generics let a function or type work with many types while keeping type safety
Written with angle brackets such as <T>
Constraints with extends limit allowed types

TypeScript.explanation: Generics avoid the any type while staying reusable.

Kotlin.question: How does Kotlin handle null safety?

key_points.point: Types are non-nullable by default; nullable types use ?
Safe call operator ?. and Elvis operator ?:
This prevents most NullPointerExceptions at compile time

Kotlin.explanation: Null safety is part of Kotlin's type system.

Kotlin.question: What are data classes in Kotlin?

key_points.point: Classes meant to hold data
equals, hashCode, toString and copy are generated automatically
Support destructuring declarations

Kotlin.explanation: Data classes remove boilerplate for model objects.

Kotlin.question: What are coroutines and why use them on Android?

key_points.point: Lightweight concurrency for asynchronous work
suspend functions pause without blocking a thread
Scopes and dispatchers (e.g. Main, IO) keep the UI responsive

Kotlin.explanation: Coroutines make async code sequential and cancellable.

key_points.point: An optional either holds a value or nil
Unwrap safely with if let or guard let
Force unwrapping with ! can crash if the value is nil

Swift.question: What is the difference between a struct and a class in Swift?

key_points.point: Structs are value types; classes are reference types
Classes support inheritance; structs do not
Structs are preferred for simple models (and in SwiftUI)

Swift.explanation: Value semantics avoid shared mutable state.

Swift.question: Explain protocols and protocol extensions in Swift.

key_points.point: A protocol defines required methods and properties
Types adopt protocols to conform
Extensions can provide default implementations (protocol-oriented programming)

HTML.question: What is semantic HTML and why does it matter?

key_points.point: Using elements that describe meaning (header, nav, article, footer)
Improves accessibility for screen readers
Helps SEO and maintainability

HTML.explanation: Meaningful markup helps users, assistive tools and search engines.

HTML.question: How do you make an HTML form accessible?

key_points.point: Every input has an associated label
Use correct input types and required/validation attributes
Keyboard navigation and clear error messages

HTML.explanation: Accessible forms can be used without a mouse or sight.

HTML.question: What is the difference between block and inline elements, and how does the DOM relate to HTML?

key_points.point: Block elements start on a new line and take full width; inline elements flow in text
The browser parses HTML into a DOM tree
JavaScript reads and changes the DOM

HTML.explanation: The DOM is the live object model of the page.

CSS.question: Explain the CSS box model.

key_points.point: Content, padding, border and margin
box-sizing: border-box includes padding and border in the width
Margins can collapse vertically

CSS.explanation: The box model controls an element's size and spacing.

CSS.question: When would you use Flexbox and when would you use Grid?

key_points.point: Flexbox is for one-dimensional layouts (row or column)
Grid is for two-dimensional layouts (rows and columns)
They are often combined

CSS.explanation: Pick the tool by the dimension of the layout.

CSS.question: How does CSS specificity work?

key_points.point: Inline styles beat IDs, which beat classes, which beat elements
When specificity ties, the later rule wins
!important overrides normal rules and should be used sparingly

CSS.explanation: Specificity decides which conflicting rule applies.

Bootstrap.question: How does the Bootstrap grid system work?

key_points.point: A 12-column layout with containers, rows and columns
Breakpoint classes (sm, md, lg) make layouts responsive
Built on Flexbox

Bootstrap.explanation: The grid adapts columns to screen size.

Bootstrap.question: How would you customise Bootstrap's look for a project?

key_points.point: Override variables (e.g. Sass variables) for colours and spacing
Add custom CSS after Bootstrap's CSS
Import only the components you need

Bootstrap.explanation: Theming through variables avoids fighting the framework.

Bootstrap.question: What are the trade-offs of using a CSS framework like Bootstrap?

key_points.point: Faster development and consistent components
Larger CSS size and a generic look if not customised
Need to learn and override its conventions

Tailwind CSS.question: What does utility-first mean in Tailwind CSS?

key_points.point: Styles are built from small single-purpose classes in the markup
Less custom CSS to write and name
Only the classes you actually use are generated in the final CSS

Tailwind CSS.explanation: Utilities keep styling close to the markup.

Tailwind CSS.question: How do you build responsive and hover styles in Tailwind?

key_points.point: Breakpoint prefixes such as md: and lg:
State variants such as hover: and focus:
Mobile-first: unprefixed classes apply to all sizes

Tailwind CSS.explanation: Variants express responsive and interactive styles inline.

Tailwind CSS.question: How do you keep Tailwind code maintainable in a large project?

key_points.point: Extract repeated patterns into components
Use the config file for design tokens (colours, spacing)
@apply for shared class groups when appropriate

Tailwind CSS.explanation: Components and a shared theme prevent class-list sprawl.

React.question: What is the difference between props and state in React?

key_points.point: Props are passed from the parent and are read-only
State is managed inside the component and can change
Changing state triggers a re-render

React.explanation: Data flows down through props; state holds local data.

React.question: Explain the useEffect hook and its dependency array.

key_points.point: useEffect runs side effects after render (fetching, subscriptions)
The dependency array controls when it re-runs
Return a cleanup function to undo the effect

React.explanation: Effects sync components with external systems.

React.question: How would you improve the performance of a slow React application?

key_points.point: Avoid unnecessary re-renders with React.memo, useMemo and useCallback
Split code and lazy-load components
Measure with the profiler and virtualise long lists

React.explanation: Measure first, then reduce work per render.

React Native.question: How is React Native different from React for the web?

key_points.point: Renders native mobile components instead of HTML elements
Styling uses JavaScript objects (StyleSheet) with Flexbox
One codebase for Android and iOS

React Native.explanation: Same React model, different rendering target.

React Native.question: How do you handle navigation between screens in React Native?

key_points.point: Use a navigation library such as React Navigation
Stack, tab and drawer navigators
Pass parameters between screens

React Native.explanation: Navigators manage screen history and transitions.

React Native.question: What causes performance problems in React Native apps and how do you fix them?

key_points.point: Too much work on the JavaScript thread / unnecessary re-renders
Use FlatList for long lists instead of ScrollView
Optimise images and avoid heavy computations during animations

React Native.explanation: Keep the JS thread free and render lists efficiently.

Angular.question: What are components and modules in Angular?

key_points.point: A component combines a template, styles and a TypeScript class
Modules (or standalone components) group and configure features
Components form a tree that builds the UI

Angular.question: How does dependency injection work in Angular?

key_points.point: Services are provided and injected into constructors
Providers define scope (root or component level)
Makes code testable and reusable

Angular.explanation: DI decouples components from the services they use.

Angular.question: Explain change detection in Angular and how OnPush helps.

key_points.point: Angular checks component bindings for changes after events
OnPush only checks when inputs change or events occur in the component
Reduces unnecessary checks and improves performance

Angular.explanation: OnPush narrows when change detection runs.

Vue.question: What are the main parts of a Vue single-file component?

key_points.point: A template, a script and a style block
Reactive data drives the template
Directives such as v-if, v-for and v-model

Vue.explanation: SFCs keep markup, logic and styles together.

Vue.question: What is the difference between computed properties and watchers in Vue?

key_points.point: Computed properties derive values and are cached
Watchers run side effects when data changes
Prefer computed for derived data

Vue.explanation: Computed for values, watchers for effects.

Vue.question: How would you manage shared state in a larger Vue application?

key_points.point: Use a store such as Pinia (or Vuex)
Keep a single source of truth with actions to change state
Use props/events for local communication and the store for global state

Vue.explanation: Centralised stores make shared state predictable.

Node.js.question: What is Node.js and why is it good for I/O-heavy applications?

key_points.point: A JavaScript runtime outside the browser (built on V8)
Non-blocking, event-driven I/O
Handles many concurrent connections efficiently

Node.js.explanation: Node excels when work is mostly waiting on I/O.

Node.js.question: How do you handle errors in asynchronous Node.js code?

key_points.point: try/catch with async/await
.catch on promises and error-first callbacks
Centralised error-handling middleware and logging

Node.js.explanation: Unhandled rejections can crash a Node process.

Node.js.question: Why should you avoid CPU-heavy work on the Node.js main thread, and what are the alternatives?

key_points.point: It blocks the event loop and delays every other request
Use worker threads or child processes
Or move the work to a separate service or queue

Node.js.explanation: Keep the event loop free for I/O.

Django.question: Describe Django's MVT architecture.

key_points.point: Models define data and map to database tables
Views handle requests and return responses
Templates render HTML

Django.explanation: MVT separates data, logic and presentation.

Django.question: What are Django migrations and how do you use them?

key_points.point: Migrations version changes to the database schema
makemigrations creates them; migrate applies them
They are committed with the code and applied in each environment

Django.explanation: Migrations keep the schema in sync with models.

Django.question: How do you avoid the N+1 query problem in the Django ORM?

key_points.point: N+1 happens when related objects are fetched one query at a time
select_related for foreign keys (SQL join)
prefetch_related for many-to-many and reverse relations

Django.explanation: Batching related queries keeps pages fast.

FastAPI.question: What are the main advantages of FastAPI?

key_points.point: Validation and serialization with Pydantic models
Automatic interactive API documentation (OpenAPI / Swagger)
Built on type hints and supports async

FastAPI.explanation: Type hints drive validation and documentation.

FastAPI.question: What is dependency injection in FastAPI and how is it used?

key_points.point: Depends declares reusable dependencies for endpoints
Common uses: database sessions, authentication, settings
Dependencies can be overridden in tests

FastAPI.explanation: Dependencies share setup logic across endpoints.

FastAPI.question: When should a FastAPI endpoint be async def versus def?

key_points.point: async def for non-blocking I/O with async libraries
def endpoints run in a thread pool, suitable for blocking code
Blocking calls inside async def stall the event loop

FastAPI.explanation: Match the endpoint style to the libraries it calls.

Spring Boot.question: What does Spring Boot provide on top of the Spring framework?

key_points.point: Auto-configuration based on dependencies
Starter dependencies and an embedded server
Production features such as Actuator and externalised configuration

Spring Boot.question: How do you build a REST endpoint in Spring Boot?

key_points.point: @RestController with @GetMapping / @PostMapping
@RequestBody and @PathVariable for input
Services and repositories hold business logic and data access

Spring Boot.explanation: Controllers stay thin; services hold logic.

Spring Boot.question: How does transaction management work in Spring?

key_points.point: @Transactional wraps a method in a transaction
Rollback on runtime exceptions by default
Propagation and isolation levels control behaviour

REST API.question: What are the main HTTP methods and what are they used for in a REST API?

key_points.point: GET reads, POST creates
PUT/PATCH update, DELETE removes
Resources are identified by URLs

REST API.question: Explain common HTTP status codes and when to use them.

key_points.point: 2xx success: 200 OK, 201 Created, 204 No Content
4xx client errors: 400, 401, 403, 404, 422
5xx server errors such as 500 and 503

REST API.explanation: Correct codes make APIs predictable for clients.

REST API.question: What does idempotency mean in REST, and which methods are idempotent?

key_points.point: Repeating the same request has the same effect as doing it once
GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not, and PATCH is not guaranteed to be
Important for safe retries

REST API.explanation: Idempotency allows clients to retry safely.

GraphQL.question: How is GraphQL different from REST?

key_points.point: Clients request exactly the fields they need
Usually a single endpoint
A typed schema describes the API

GraphQL.explanation: GraphQL shifts query shape to the client.

GraphQL.question: What are queries, mutations and resolvers in GraphQL?

key_points.point: Queries read data
Mutations change data
Resolvers are functions that fetch the data for each field

GraphQL.explanation: Resolvers connect the schema to data sources.

GraphQL.question: What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL and how is it solved?

key_points.point: Nested resolvers trigger one query per item
Batching with DataLoader
Caching within a request

GraphQL.explanation: Batching collapses many small queries into one.

SQL.question: What is the difference between INNER JOIN and LEFT JOIN?

key_points.point: INNER JOIN returns only rows that match in both tables
LEFT JOIN returns all rows from the left table
Missing matches are filled with NULL

SQL.explanation: LEFT JOIN keeps unmatched rows from the left side.

SQL.question: What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?

key_points.point: WHERE filters rows before grouping
HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY
HAVING can use aggregate functions like COUNT or SUM

SQL.explanation: Filter rows with WHERE, groups with HAVING.

SQL.question: How do indexes improve query performance, and what are their costs?

key_points.point: Indexes (often B-trees) let the database find rows without scanning the table
They slow down inserts and updates and use storage
Index columns used in WHERE, JOIN and ORDER BY; check with EXPLAIN

SQL.explanation: Indexes trade write cost for read speed.

SQLite.question: What is SQLite and when is it a good choice?

key_points.point: A serverless database stored in a single file
Good for mobile apps, prototypes, tests and small tools
Not ideal for many concurrent writers

SQLite.explanation: SQLite is simple and embedded, with limited write concurrency.

SQLite.question: How does SQLite handle data types?

key_points.point: Dynamic typing with storage classes (INTEGER, REAL, TEXT, BLOB, NULL)
Column type affinity guides conversion
STRICT tables enforce types

SQLite.explanation: SQLite is more flexible with types than most databases.

SQLite.question: How do transactions and locking work in SQLite?

key_points.point: Writes lock the database; one writer at a time
WAL mode lets readers continue while writing
Group many writes in one transaction for speed

SQLite.explanation: Batching writes and WAL improve concurrency.

Firebase.question: What services does Firebase provide for app developers?

key_points.point: Authentication
Databases: Firestore and Realtime Database
Hosting, storage and cloud functions

Firebase.explanation: Firebase is a managed backend for apps.

Firebase.question: How should you structure data in Firestore?

key_points.point: Collections of documents with fields
Model data for your queries; denormalise where needed
Use subcollections for related data

Firebase.explanation: NoSQL design starts from access patterns.

Firebase.question: Why are Firebase security rules important?

key_points.point: Clients talk to the database directly, so rules enforce access
Check authentication and ownership in rules
Validate data shape and test rules

Firebase.explanation: Without rules, any client could read or write data.

AWS.question: What are EC2 and S3 used for?

key_points.point: EC2 provides virtual servers
S3 stores objects (files) in buckets
Pay for what you use and scale as needed

AWS.explanation: EC2 is compute; S3 is storage.

AWS.question: What is IAM and what is the principle of least privilege?

key_points.point: IAM manages users, roles and permissions
Grant only the permissions that are needed
Prefer roles over long-lived access keys

AWS.explanation: Least privilege limits the impact of mistakes and breaches.

AWS.question: How would you design a highly available web application on AWS?

key_points.point: Run across multiple Availability Zones
Use a load balancer and auto scaling
Managed database with replicas and backups

Azure.question: What are resource groups in Azure?

key_points.point: Logical containers for related resources
Manage access, policies and costs together
Deleting a group deletes its resources

Azure.explanation: Resource groups organise a solution's resources.

Azure.question: When would you use Azure App Service versus a virtual machine?

key_points.point: App Service is managed hosting (PaaS) for web apps
VMs give full control of the OS (IaaS)
Managed services reduce maintenance

Azure.explanation: Choose the least operational burden that fits.

Azure.question: How do you manage identity and secrets in Azure?

key_points.point: Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) for identity and RBAC
Managed identities avoid storing credentials
Key Vault stores secrets and keys

Azure.explanation: Avoid secrets in code; use identities and Key Vault.

GCP.question: What are Compute Engine and Cloud Storage in Google Cloud?

key_points.point: Compute Engine provides virtual machines
Cloud Storage stores objects in buckets
Resources live inside projects

GCP.explanation: Projects organise GCP resources and billing.

GCP.question: When would you use Cloud Run?

key_points.point: Runs containers without managing servers
Scales automatically, including to zero
Good for stateless HTTP services

GCP.question: How does IAM work in Google Cloud?

key_points.point: Roles bundle permissions and are granted to principals
Service accounts are identities for workloads
Grant at the narrowest scope (least privilege)

GCP.explanation: Policies bind roles to identities on resources.

Docker.question: What is the difference between a Docker image and a container?

key_points.point: An image is a read-only template
A container is a running instance of an image
Many containers can run from one image

Docker.explanation: Images are built; containers are run.

Docker.question: How do you write an efficient Dockerfile?

key_points.point: Use a small base image
Order layers to use the build cache (copy dependencies first)
Multi-stage builds and a .dockerignore

Docker.explanation: Smaller images build and deploy faster and are safer.

Docker.question: How do containers persist data and communicate with each other?

key_points.point: Volumes (or bind mounts) persist data beyond the container
User-defined networks let containers reach each other by name
Docker Compose defines multi-container setups

Docker.explanation: Containers are ephemeral; volumes hold state.

Kubernetes.question: What are Pods, Deployments and Services in Kubernetes?

key_points.point: A Pod runs one or more containers
A Deployment manages replicas and rolling updates
A Service gives Pods a stable network address

Kubernetes.explanation: These are the core building blocks.

Kubernetes.question: How do you pass configuration and secrets to applications in Kubernetes?

key_points.point: ConfigMaps for non-sensitive configuration
Secrets for sensitive values
Expose them as environment variables or mounted files

Kubernetes.explanation: Keep configuration out of container images.

Kubernetes.question: How does Kubernetes keep an application healthy and scaled?

key_points.point: Liveness and readiness probes
Self-healing: failed Pods are restarted or replaced
Horizontal Pod Autoscaler scales on metrics

Kubernetes.explanation: Kubernetes reconciles to the desired state.

Terraform.question: What is Terraform and what problem does it solve?

key_points.point: Infrastructure as code: infrastructure defined in configuration files
Repeatable, version-controlled environments
Works with many providers (AWS, Azure, GCP)

Terraform.question: What is the Terraform state file and why is it important?

key_points.point: State maps configuration to real resources
Store state remotely with locking for teams
State can contain secrets, so protect it

Terraform.explanation: State lets Terraform plan accurate changes.

Terraform.question: How do you structure Terraform for multiple environments?

key_points.point: Reusable modules
Separate state per environment (workspaces or directories)
Variables and tfvars per environment; review plans before apply

Terraform.explanation: Modules plus isolated state keep environments safe.

Jenkins.question: What is Jenkins used for?

key_points.point: Automating builds, tests and deployments (CI/CD)
Jobs or pipelines triggered by events such as commits
Extensible through plugins

Jenkins.explanation: Jenkins is a CI/CD automation server.

Jenkins.question: What is a Jenkinsfile and why use pipeline as code?

key_points.point: A Jenkinsfile defines the pipeline in the repository
Stages and steps (declarative syntax)
Version-controlled and reviewable like code

Jenkins.question: How do you handle credentials securely in Jenkins?

key_points.point: Use the Jenkins credentials store
Inject credentials with bindings instead of hard-coding
Mask secrets in logs and restrict access

Jenkins.explanation: Secrets must never appear in code or logs.

CI/CD.question: What is the difference between continuous integration and continuous delivery?

key_points.point: CI: frequently merge code and run automated builds and tests
CD: code is always in a deployable state and released automatically or with one click
Catches problems early

CI/CD.explanation: CI keeps code healthy; CD keeps it shippable.

CI/CD.question: What stages would a typical CI/CD pipeline have?

key_points.point: Build
Test (unit, integration) and code quality checks
Deploy to staging, then production

CI/CD.question: What deployment strategies reduce risk in production?

key_points.point: Blue-green deployments
Canary or rolling releases
Feature flags and fast rollback

CI/CD.explanation: Release gradually and be able to undo quickly.

Linux.question: How do Linux file permissions work?

key_points.point: Read, write and execute permissions
For owner, group and others
Changed with chmod and chown

Linux.explanation: Permissions control who can do what with a file.

Linux.question: How would you find which process is using a lot of CPU or a specific port?

key_points.point: top or htop for CPU and memory
ps to list processes
ss, netstat or lsof for ports

Linux.question: How do services and logs work on a modern Linux system?

key_points.point: systemd manages services with systemctl
Logs via journalctl and /var/log
Enable services to start at boot

Linux.explanation: systemd starts, supervises and logs services.

Networking.question: What is the difference between TCP and UDP?

key_points.point: TCP is connection-oriented and reliable
UDP is connectionless, with lower overhead and no delivery or ordering guarantee
Examples: HTTP uses TCP; video calls and DNS often use UDP

Networking.question: What happens when you type a URL into a browser?

key_points.point: DNS resolves the domain to an IP address
TCP connection and TLS handshake for HTTPS
HTTP request and response; the browser renders the page
CIDR such as /24 gives the number of network bits
Subnets split a network into smaller ranges
Used for organisation, security and routing

Monitoring.question: What is the difference between metrics, logs and traces?

key_points.point: Metrics are numeric measurements over time
Logs are records of events
Traces follow a request across services

Monitoring.question: How do you design useful alerts?

key_points.point: Alert on symptoms that affect users (errors, latency)
Avoid noisy alerts that cause fatigue
Each alert should be actionable

Monitoring.explanation: Good alerts are rare, relevant and actionable.

Monitoring.question: What are SLIs, SLOs and SLAs?

key_points.point: SLI: a measured indicator such as availability or latency
SLO: the target for an SLI
SLA: an agreement with consequences if missed

Git.question: What is the difference between git merge and git rebase?

key_points.point: Merge combines branches with a merge commit
Rebase replays commits onto another base for a linear history
Avoid rebasing shared branches

Git.explanation: Rebase rewrites history; merge preserves it.

Git.question: How do you resolve a merge conflict?

key_points.point: Git marks conflicting sections in the files
Edit to the correct result, then add and commit
Run tests and communicate with whoever made the other change

Git.question: Describe a branching workflow for a team.

key_points.point: Feature branches for each change
Pull requests with code review
Protected main branch and CI checks before merging

Git.explanation: Branches plus review keep main stable.

JIRA.question: How is JIRA used in software teams?

key_points.point: Tracking issues such as stories, tasks and bugs
Boards for workflow (to do, in progress, done)
Planning sprints and reporting progress

JIRA.explanation: JIRA makes work visible and trackable.

JIRA.question: What makes a good bug report?

key_points.point: Clear title and steps to reproduce
Expected versus actual behaviour
Environment details, screenshots or logs, and priority

JIRA.question: How do you use JIRA to track a sprint's progress?

key_points.point: Sprint board and burndown chart
Estimates such as story points and velocity
Keep statuses up to date and review in standups and retrospectives

Machine Learning.question: What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised learning?

key_points.point: Supervised learning uses labelled data
Unsupervised learning finds structure in unlabelled data
Examples: classification/regression vs clustering

Machine Learning.question: What are overfitting and underfitting, and how do you address them?

key_points.point: Overfitting: the model fits training data but generalises poorly
Underfitting: the model is too simple to capture patterns
Use validation, regularisation, more data or a different model complexity

Machine Learning.explanation: Aim for good performance on unseen data.

Machine Learning.question: How do you evaluate a classification model on an imbalanced dataset?

key_points.point: Accuracy can be misleading
Use precision, recall, F1 and the confusion matrix
ROC-AUC or PR-AUC, and resampling or class weights

Machine Learning.explanation: Choose metrics that reflect the minority class.

Deep Learning.question: What is a neural network?

key_points.point: Layers of neurons connected by weights
Activation functions add non-linearity
Weights are learned from data by training

Deep Learning.explanation: Stacked non-linear layers learn complex functions.

Deep Learning.question: How does backpropagation work?

key_points.point: Compute the loss for a prediction
Gradients are computed backwards with the chain rule
An optimiser such as gradient descent or Adam updates the weights

Deep Learning.explanation: Backprop tells each weight how to change.

Deep Learning.question: How do you reduce overfitting in deep learning models?

key_points.point: Dropout and weight decay
Data augmentation and more data
Early stopping on a validation set

NLP.question: What is tokenisation in NLP?

key_points.point: Splitting text into units called tokens
Tokens can be words, subwords or characters
It is a first step before models can process text

NLP.explanation: Models work on tokens, not raw text.

key_points.point: Words are represented as dense numeric vectors
Similar meanings are close together in vector space
Examples: Word2Vec, GloVe, or contextual embeddings from transformers

NLP.question: What is attention in transformer models?

key_points.point: Each token weighs how relevant every other token is
Computed with queries, keys and values
Captures long-range context and runs in parallel

NLP.explanation: Attention replaced recurrence for sequence modelling.

Computer Vision.question: What is a convolutional neural network (CNN)?

key_points.point: Convolution filters detect local patterns such as edges
Pooling reduces spatial size
Deeper layers learn higher-level features

Computer Vision.explanation: CNNs exploit the spatial structure of images.

Computer Vision.question: What is data augmentation and why use it for images?

key_points.point: Create modified copies of training images
Examples: flips, rotations, crops, colour changes
Improves generalisation and reduces overfitting

Computer Vision.question: What is the difference between image classification, object detection and segmentation?

key_points.point: Classification assigns one label to an image
Detection finds objects with bounding boxes
Segmentation labels each pixel

Computer Vision.explanation: Each task gives increasingly detailed output.

TensorFlow.question: How do you build and train a simple model with TensorFlow Keras?

key_points.point: Define layers with Sequential or the functional API
compile with an optimiser, loss and metrics
fit on training data and evaluate on test data

TensorFlow.question: What are callbacks in Keras training?

key_points.point: Hooks that run during training (e.g. after each epoch)
EarlyStopping and ModelCheckpoint
Learning-rate scheduling and logging (TensorBoard)

TensorFlow.question: How do you build an efficient input pipeline in TensorFlow?

key_points.point: tf.data Dataset API
map, batch, shuffle and prefetch
Keeps the GPU busy instead of waiting for data

TensorFlow.explanation: Input pipelines often limit training speed.

PyTorch.question: What are tensors and autograd in PyTorch?

key_points.point: Tensors are multi-dimensional arrays that can run on a GPU
Autograd records operations to compute gradients
backward() computes the gradients

PyTorch.question: Describe a typical PyTorch training loop.

key_points.point: Forward pass and loss computation
zero_grad, backward, then optimizer.step
Loop over batches from a DataLoader for several epochs

PyTorch.question: What is the difference between model.train() and model.eval(), and why use torch.no_grad()?

key_points.point: train/eval switch layers like dropout and batch norm
no_grad disables gradient tracking during inference
This saves memory and computation

PyTorch.explanation: Inference mode differs from training mode.

Scikit-learn.question: Describe the basic scikit-learn workflow.

key_points.point: Split data into training and test sets
fit the model and predict
Evaluate with metrics

Scikit-learn.explanation: Estimators share a consistent fit/predict API.

Scikit-learn.question: Why use Pipelines in scikit-learn?

key_points.point: Chain preprocessing and the model into one object
Prevents data leakage during cross-validation
Simplifies tuning and deployment

Scikit-learn.explanation: Pipelines make preprocessing part of the model.

Scikit-learn.question: How do you tune hyperparameters in scikit-learn?

key_points.point: GridSearchCV or RandomizedSearchCV
Uses cross-validation to score each combination
Keep a separate test set for the final evaluation

Scikit-learn.explanation: Never tune on the test set.

Pandas.question: What are a Series and a DataFrame in Pandas?

key_points.point: A Series is a one-dimensional labelled array
A DataFrame is a two-dimensional table of columns
Both have an index

Pandas.explanation: DataFrames are the core tabular structure.

Pandas.question: How do you handle missing data in Pandas?

key_points.point: Detect with isna / isnull
Drop with dropna or fill with fillna
Choose a strategy based on the data (mean, median, forward fill)

Pandas.explanation: The right strategy depends on why data is missing.

Pandas.question: Explain groupby and merge in Pandas.

key_points.point: groupby splits data into groups, applies a function and combines results
Aggregations such as sum, mean and count
merge joins DataFrames on keys (inner, left, outer)

NumPy.question: Why are NumPy arrays faster than Python lists for numeric work?

key_points.point: Stored in contiguous memory with a single data type
Vectorised operations run in compiled code
No Python-level loops over elements
Operations between arrays of different shapes
Smaller dimensions are stretched to match without copying
Follows rules comparing dimensions from the right

NumPy.question: What is the difference between a view and a copy in NumPy?

key_points.point: Basic slicing returns a view that shares memory
Changing a view changes the original array
Use .copy() for an independent array; fancy indexing returns a copy

NumPy.explanation: Views are fast but can cause surprising side effects.

Statistics.question: What is the difference between mean, median and mode?

key_points.point: Mean is the average
Median is the middle value and is robust to outliers
Mode is the most frequent value

Statistics.explanation: Pick the measure that fits the distribution.

Statistics.question: What is a p-value and how is it used in hypothesis testing?

key_points.point: Probability of results at least this extreme if the null hypothesis is true
Compared with a significance level such as 0.05
A small p-value is evidence against the null, not proof

Statistics.explanation: P-values measure surprise under the null hypothesis.

Statistics.question: Explain the difference between correlation and causation.

key_points.point: Correlation measures how variables move together
Causation means one variable changes the other
Confounders can create correlation; experiments help establish causation

Statistics.explanation: Correlation alone does not prove cause.

Data Analysis.question: What steps do you follow in a typical data analysis?

key_points.point: Define the question or goal
Collect, clean and explore the data
Analyse and communicate findings with visuals

Data Analysis.explanation: Analysis starts with a clear question.

Data Analysis.question: How do you handle outliers in a dataset?

key_points.point: Detect with plots or rules such as IQR or z-score
Investigate whether they are errors or real values
Remove, cap or keep them and document the choice

Data Analysis.explanation: Outliers can be mistakes or the most interesting points.

Data Analysis.question: How would you measure whether a product change improved results?

key_points.point: Define a clear success metric
Run an A/B test with control and treatment groups
Check statistical significance and sample size

Data Analysis.explanation: Controlled experiments isolate the effect of a change.

Excel.question: What is the difference between relative and absolute cell references?

key_points.point: Relative references change when a formula is copied
Absolute references use $ to stay fixed
Mixed references fix only the row or column

Excel.question: How do you look up values from another table in Excel?

key_points.point: VLOOKUP or XLOOKUP
INDEX with MATCH for flexible lookups
Use exact match and handle errors (IFERROR)

Excel.question: How do pivot tables help analyse data?

key_points.point: Summarise large datasets by grouping
Rows, columns, values and filters
Aggregations such as sum, count and average, updated by refreshing

Excel.explanation: Pivot tables are quick, flexible summaries.

Power BI.question: What are the main steps to build a Power BI report?

key_points.point: Connect to and import data
Transform data in Power Query
Build visuals and publish the report

Power BI.question: Why is data modelling important in Power BI?

key_points.point: Relationships between tables
Star schema with fact and dimension tables
Correct, fast calculations and filtering

Power BI.explanation: A good model makes measures simple and fast.

Power BI.question: What is DAX, and what is the difference between a measure and a calculated column?

key_points.point: DAX is the formula language of Power BI
Measures are calculated at query time in the current filter context
Calculated columns are computed per row and stored

Tableau.question: What is the difference between dimensions and measures in Tableau?

key_points.point: Dimensions are categorical fields used to group
Measures are numeric values that are aggregated
They determine how charts are built

Tableau.question: How do you create a calculated field in Tableau and when would you use one?

key_points.point: Create a new field with a formula
Used for ratios, conditions or custom categories
Can be row-level or aggregate

Tableau.explanation: Calculations extend the data without changing the source.

Tableau.question: What makes an effective dashboard?

key_points.point: Designed for a clear audience and question
Few, well-chosen charts with a clear layout
Interactive filters and performance kept in mind

Tableau.explanation: Dashboards should answer questions at a glance.

Data Structures.question: What is the difference between an array and a linked list?

key_points.point: Arrays allow O(1) access by index
Linked lists insert or delete in O(1) once you hold the node, but finding it takes O(n)
Arrays use contiguous memory; linked lists use nodes with pointers

Data Structures.explanation: Choose by the operations you need most.

Data Structures.question: How does a hash table work?

key_points.point: A hash function maps keys to buckets
Collisions are handled by chaining or open addressing
Average O(1) insert and lookup

Data Structures.question: When would you use a heap, and what are its operation costs?

key_points.point: A heap keeps the minimum or maximum at the top
Insert and remove-top are O(log n); peek is O(1)
Used for priority queues, scheduling and top-k problems

Data Structures.explanation: Heaps efficiently track the extreme element.

key_points.point: Describes how running time or memory grows with input size
It is an upper bound on growth, most often quoted for the worst case
Examples: O(1), O(log n), O(n), O(n^2)

Algorithms.question: How does binary search work, and what does it require?

key_points.point: Requires sorted data
Compare with the middle element and discard half each step
O(log n) time

Algorithms.explanation: Halving the search space is very efficient.

Algorithms.question: What is dynamic programming? Give an example.

key_points.point: Breaks a problem into overlapping subproblems
Stores results to avoid recomputation (memoisation or tabulation)
Examples: Fibonacci, knapsack, longest common subsequence

Selenium.question: What is Selenium WebDriver used for?

key_points.point: Automating browser interactions for testing
Locating elements by ID, CSS selector or XPath
Supports multiple browsers and languages

Selenium.question: What is the difference between implicit and explicit waits in Selenium?

key_points.point: Implicit waits apply a global timeout for finding elements
Explicit waits wait for a specific condition
Explicit waits reduce flaky tests; avoid fixed sleeps

Selenium.explanation: Wait for conditions, not fixed times.

Selenium.question: What is the Page Object Model and why use it?

key_points.point: Each page is represented by a class with its elements and actions
Tests call page methods instead of raw locators
Easier maintenance when the UI changes

Selenium.explanation: POM separates test logic from page details.

Figma.question: What are components and variants in Figma?

key_points.point: Components are reusable design elements
Instances update when the main component changes
Variants group states such as default, hover and disabled

Figma.question: What is Auto Layout in Figma and why is it useful?

key_points.point: Frames resize automatically to their content
Controls spacing, padding and direction
Makes responsive and maintainable designs easier

Figma.explanation: Auto Layout behaves like CSS Flexbox.

Figma.question: How do you hand off a Figma design to developers?

key_points.point: Use consistent styles and components (design tokens)
Developers inspect measurements, CSS and assets
Annotate behaviour and states, and stay in contact

Adobe XD.question: What can you do with Adobe XD in a design workflow?

key_points.point: Design screens on artboards
Create interactive prototypes
Share designs for feedback

Adobe XD.question: How do components and states help in Adobe XD?

key_points.point: Reuse elements across screens
States show variations such as hover
Changes to the main component update everywhere

Adobe XD.explanation: Components save time and keep consistency.

Adobe XD.question: How do you test a prototype with users?

key_points.point: Define tasks and goals for the test
Observe users and collect feedback
Iterate on the design based on findings

Wireframing.question: What is a wireframe and why create one?

key_points.point: A low-fidelity layout of a screen
Focuses on structure and content, not visual style
Cheap to change and good for early feedback

Wireframing.question: How do you decide what goes on a wireframe?

key_points.point: User goals and key tasks
Information hierarchy and priority
Navigation and user flow between screens

Wireframing.question: How do wireframes, mockups and prototypes differ?

key_points.point: Wireframes show structure (low fidelity)
Mockups add visual design (high fidelity, static)
Prototypes add interaction

Wireframing.explanation: Fidelity and interactivity increase step by step.

Prototyping.question: What is the purpose of a prototype?

key_points.point: Simulate how the product works before building it
Test ideas with users
Reduce cost by finding problems early

Prototyping.question: When would you use a low-fidelity versus a high-fidelity prototype?

key_points.point: Low fidelity for early ideas and flows
High fidelity for detailed interaction and visual testing
Match fidelity to the question you need answered

Prototyping.explanation: Don't polish what you're still exploring.

Prototyping.question: How do you turn usability test results into prototype improvements?

key_points.point: Group findings and identify patterns
Prioritise by severity and frequency
Change the prototype and test again

User Research.question: What is the difference between qualitative and quantitative user research?

key_points.point: Qualitative explores why (interviews, observation)
Quantitative measures how many or how much (surveys, analytics)
They are often combined

User Research.explanation: Use both to understand and measure.

User Research.question: How do you run a good user interview?

key_points.point: Prepare goals and an interview guide
Ask open, non-leading questions
Listen, take notes and synthesise findings

User Research.question: What are personas and journey maps, and how are they used?

key_points.point: Personas summarise user types from research
Journey maps show steps, emotions and pain points over time
They guide design decisions and team alignment

User Research.explanation: They turn research into shared understanding.

key_points.point: A shared set of reusable components and guidelines
Includes design tokens such as colours, typography and spacing
Keeps products consistent across teams
Named values for design decisions
Examples: colours, font sizes, spacing, radii
Shared between design tools and code

Design Systems.question: How do you keep a design system adopted and up to date?

key_points.point: Clear documentation and usage examples
Versioning and a contribution process
Collaborate with product teams and gather feedback

Design Systems.explanation: Design systems are products for internal users.

Agile.question: What are the core ideas of Agile?

key_points.point: Deliver working software in small increments
Collaborate with customers and respond to change
Regular feedback and continuous improvement

Agile.explanation: Agile values adaptation over rigid plans.

key_points.point: Sprint planning selects work from the backlog
Daily stand-ups to track progress and blockers
Review and retrospective at the end

Agile.question: How do you write a good user story?

key_points.point: As a <user>, I want <goal> so that <benefit>
Clear acceptance criteria
Small, independent and testable (INVEST)

Agile.explanation: Stories describe value from the user's view.

Market Research.question: What is the difference between primary and secondary market research?

key_points.point: Primary research collects new data directly (surveys, interviews)
Secondary research uses existing data (reports, studies)
Secondary is cheaper; primary is more specific

Market Research.explanation: Combine both for a complete picture.

Market Research.question: How would you analyse competitors?

key_points.point: Identify direct and indirect competitors
Compare products, pricing, positioning and customers
Summarise strengths and weaknesses (e.g. SWOT)

Market Research.explanation: Competitor analysis reveals gaps and threats.

Market Research.question: How do you estimate the size of a market?

key_points.point: TAM, SAM and SOM
Top-down from industry data or bottom-up from units and price
State assumptions and check them

Financial Modeling.question: What are the three main financial statements?

key_points.point: Income statement shows revenue, costs and profit
Balance sheet shows assets, liabilities and equity
Cash flow statement shows cash movements

Financial Modeling.question: How do you build revenue forecasts in a financial model?

key_points.point: Identify revenue drivers such as volume and price
Base assumptions on historical data and research
Keep inputs separate and run scenarios

Financial Modeling.question: Explain a discounted cash flow (DCF) valuation.

key_points.point: Forecast future free cash flows
Discount them with a rate such as WACC
Add a terminal value and sum the present values

SEO.question: What are on-page SEO factors?

key_points.point: Relevant content and keywords
Title tags, meta descriptions and headings
Internal links and image alt text

SEO.explanation: On-page SEO is what you control on the page.

SEO.question: How do you do keyword research?

key_points.point: Find terms your audience searches for
Consider search volume, competition and intent
Target long-tail keywords where relevant

SEO.question: What is technical SEO?

key_points.point: Making pages crawlable and indexable (sitemaps, robots.txt)
Fast, mobile-friendly pages
Clean URLs, HTTPS and structured data

SEO.explanation: Technical SEO helps search engines read the site.

Google Analytics.question: What does Google Analytics measure?

key_points.point: Visitors, sessions and page views
Traffic sources
User behaviour and conversions

Google Analytics.explanation: Analytics shows who visits and what they do.

Google Analytics.question: What are events and conversions in Google Analytics 4?

key_points.point: Events record user interactions
Conversions (key events) are important events you mark
They measure whether users complete valuable actions

Google Analytics.question: How would you use analytics to improve a website's conversion rate?

key_points.point: Analyse the funnel to find drop-off points
Segment users by source, device or behaviour
Test changes and measure the result

Google Analytics.explanation: Find where users leave, then test fixes.

Social Media Marketing.question: How do you choose which social media platforms to use for a brand?

key_points.point: Go where the target audience is
Match the platform to the content type
Align with business goals

Social Media Marketing.explanation: Platform choice follows audience and goals.

Social Media Marketing.question: Which metrics show whether a social media campaign worked?

key_points.point: Reach and impressions
Engagement rate (likes, comments, shares)
Clicks and conversions tied to goals

Social Media Marketing.question: How would you plan a social media content calendar?

key_points.point: Set goals and content themes
Schedule posts at a consistent frequency
Review performance and adjust

Social Media Marketing.explanation: Plan, publish consistently, learn and adjust.

Content Writing.question: How do you write for a specific audience?

key_points.point: Understand the audience's needs and level
Use an appropriate tone and vocabulary
Keep a clear purpose for each piece

Content Writing.question: How do you structure content so it is easy to read online?

key_points.point: Headings and short paragraphs
Bullet points and scannable formatting
Most important information first

Content Writing.explanation: Online readers scan before they read.

Content Writing.question: How do you edit your own writing effectively?

key_points.point: Take a break, then reread with fresh eyes
Cut unnecessary words and simplify sentences
Check facts, grammar and consistency

Content Writing.explanation: Editing is where clarity is made.

Communication.question: How do you explain a technical idea to a non-technical person?

key_points.point: Avoid jargon and use simple language
Use analogies or examples
Check understanding and invite questions

Communication.explanation: Adapt the message to the listener.

Communication.question: How do you give a good status update to your team or manager?

key_points.point: Say what is done, what is next and any blockers
Be concise and specific
Raise risks early

Communication.question: How do you handle disagreement in written communication, such as code review comments?

key_points.point: Focus on the work, not the person
Explain your reasoning and ask questions
Move to a call when written discussion gets stuck

Communication.explanation: Respectful, reasoned feedback keeps teams healthy.

Problem Solving.question: How do you approach a problem you have never seen before?

key_points.point: Clarify the problem and the requirements
Break it into smaller parts
Try a simple solution first, then improve

Problem Solving.explanation: Structure turns big problems into small ones.

Problem Solving.question: How do you debug an issue you cannot reproduce easily?

key_points.point: Gather evidence from logs and reports
Form hypotheses and test them one at a time
Add logging or monitoring to catch it next time

Problem Solving.question: How do you choose between several possible solutions?

key_points.point: Define criteria such as cost, time and risk
Compare trade-offs
Decide, then review the outcome
